strengths: Addresses an important and realistic problem in offline-to-online reinforcement learning: utilizing non-curated, reward-free, multi-embodiment offline datasets to accelerate online fine-tuning without manual reward labeling.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 72 vision-based control tasks spanning 6 embodiments (22 DMControl tasks and 50 Meta-World manipulation tasks), demonstrating significant sample efficiency gains over both from-scratch baselines (DrQ-v2, DreamerV3) and prior methods using offline data (ExPLORe, R3M, UDS, JSRL-BC, iVideoGPT).

Clear diagnosis of the failure mode of naive world model fine-tuning: identifying distribution mismatch between pre-training and early online interaction distributions as the primary driver of catastrophic degradation and poor exploration.

The proposed framework (GSA) is logically structured and effective: coupling representation-based trajectory retrieval with experience rehearsal and execution guidance effectively bootstraps agent exploration.
weaknesses: Trajectory retrieval relies solely on the initial visual observation (Eq. 4). While effective in settings where visual appearance separates task instances or robot embodiments (e.g., distinct object setups in Meta-World or morphology in DMControl), this heuristic fails in multi-task environments where different tasks share identical initial states (e.g., same tabletop scene where the objective is to pick vs. push). The limitations of initial-frame-only retrieval should be discussed.

The execution guidance mechanism trains a behavior cloning (BC) policy on the retrieved offline data, despite the offline dataset containing substantial noise and mixed quality (e.g., injected Gaussian noise up to $\sigma = 2.0$). The paper lacks analysis on how BC handles low-quality trajectories and whether quality-based filtering or weighting is needed when offline data quality further degrades.

The theoretical analysis in Appendix B is largely superficial: Proposition 1 is essentially a tautology derived from the definition of the retrieved subset; Proposition 2 restates multi-task objective regularization without establishing formal forgetting bounds; and Proposition 3 directly invokes standard TRPO advantage results under the strong assumption that the guide policy is strictly better by $\delta$ across all states.

All benchmark experiments are evaluated using only 3 random seeds. While evaluating 72 visuomotor control tasks is computationally demanding, 3 seeds remains on the lower end for deep RL variance assessment.

strengths: Unusually comprehensive empirical evaluation for pixel-based reinforcement learning, spanning 72 visuomotor control tasks across 6 embodiments in DMControl and Meta-World.
Addresses an important and practical problem: effectively leveraging reward-free, multi-embodiment, and mixed-quality offline data to accelerate online visual RL fine-tuning.

Provides insightful analysis into why naive world model fine-tuning fails (distribution mismatch and catastrophic forgetting) and validates the proposed remedies (experience rehearsal and execution guidance) through thorough ablation studies.

Strong competitive performance, significantly outperforming both training-from-scratch methods (Dreamer-v3, DrQ-v2) and existing offline data utilization methods (R3M, ExPLORe, JSRL-BC, iVideoGPT) under constrained sample budgets.
High level of transparency and reproducibility, including detailed listings of per-task results, network architectures, hyperparameters, and compute resource requirements.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty of individual algorithmic components is relatively modest, combining nearest-neighbor trajectory retrieval in latent space, standard experience replay regularisation, and a variant of Jump-Start RL (JSRL) policy blending.

The retrieval mechanism relies solely on initial frame embeddings via $L_2$ distance ($e_\theta(o_{on}) - e_\theta(o_{off})$). In manipulation domains like Meta-World where initial scene layouts can look similar across different tasks, it is unclear how robustly this mechanism isolates task-relevant behavior versus irrelevant trajectories.

The theoretical analysis in Appendix B is largely tautological or directly adopts strong standard assumptions (e.g., Proposition 1 trivially holds by the definition of the $\epsilon$-filtering construct, and Proposition 3 directly applies TRPO Lemma 1 under an assumed positive advantage bound $\delta > 0$).
Only 3 random seeds are used per task; while aggregate statistics (IQM) across 72 tasks help mitigate uncertainty, variance remains noticeable on hard exploration tasks.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 72 pixel-based continuous control tasks spanning 6 embodiments (DMControl and Meta-World), which is significantly larger than typical offline-to-online RL evaluations.

Strong sample efficiency improvements under limited online interaction budgets (150k environment steps), achieving substantial gains over competitive baselines such as Dreamer v3, DrQ v2, ExPLORe, and iVideoGPT.
Clear ablation studies that isolate the contributions of the pre-trained world model, experience rehearsal, and execution guidance.

The paper addresses a practically relevant problem in offline-to-online RL: scaling policy fine-tuning from multi-embodiment, reward-free offline datasets without requiring costly task-specific reward annotation.
weaknesses: The claim of using 'non-curated' offline data is somewhat overstated: the Meta-World offline dataset is generated directly by adding Gaussian noise to task-specific TD-MPC2 policies on those exact 50 tasks. Consequently, the dataset contains noisy trajectories for the target downstream tasks, which strongly aids both nearest-neighbor retrieval and behavior cloning guidance.

The retrieval mechanism is heavily reliant on the initial frame observation distance (L2 norm in latent space). While this works when tasks have visually distinct initial scenes or robot embodiments, it would fail in settings where diverse tasks or multiple goals share identical or ambiguous initial visual observations.

Algorithmic novelty is moderate: the method largely combines existing ideas, adapting RSSM world models to multi-embodiment setups via action zero-padding, nearest-neighbor trajectory retrieval for replay, and an adaptation of Jump-Start RL (JSRL) with behavior-cloned policies.

The theoretical results presented in Appendix B are overly simplistic: Proposition 1 follows trivially by definition from thresholding distances, Proposition 2 is descriptive rather than a formal proof, and Proposition 3 is a direct corollary of the standard TRPO policy performance difference lemma.

All main experiments are run with only 3 random seeds per task; given the known stochasticity of visual reinforcement learning and offline data sampling, a larger number of seeds (e.g., 5-10) or rigorous statistical dispersion reporting across all individual benchmark tasks would make the conclusions more robust.

strengths: Extensive and thorough empirical evaluation across 72 visual continuous control tasks (22 DMControl and 50 Meta-World tasks) demonstrating consistent sample-efficiency gains over learning-from-scratch (DreamerV3, DrQ-v2) and offline-data baselines (R3M, ExPLORe, JSRL-BC, iVideoGPT).
Addresses an important and realistic problem setting: utilizing reward-free, mixed-quality, multi-embodiment visual data to bootstrap online reinforcement learning.
Well-structured ablations dissecting the contributions of pre-training, experience rehearsal, execution guidance, retrieval precision, and model scale.
Identifies and addresses key failure modes of naive world model fine-tuning (distributional shift and catastrophic forgetting during early online interaction).
weaknesses: The technical novelty is somewhat incremental, as the overall framework synthesizes existing techniques: scaling an RSSM architecture, embedding-based nearest-neighbor retrieval via Faiss on initial observations, replay buffer mixing (similar in spirit to RLPD), and behavior-cloned exploration guidance (closely related to Jump-Start RL).

The theoretical analysis in Appendix B is largely trivial: Proposition 1 is a direct tautology of filtering by distance threshold, and Proposition 2 is an immediate reformulation of Kakade & Langford (2002) CPI bounds without new theoretical insights tailored to world models.

The retrieval mechanism relies on initial observation similarity via L2 distance in latent space. This works reliably because DMControl and Meta-World have distinct visual environments per task/robot; it remains unclear how well this retrieval would scale to diverse real-world scenes or in-the-wild video datasets where initial frames do not neatly index task dynamics.

Handling of multi-embodiment is limited to zero-padding action dimensions across a few continuous control bodies in the same simulator suite, which may not translate easily to truly heterogeneous embodiment spaces.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in offline-to-online RL: utilizing non-curated, reward-free, mixed-quality, and multi-embodiment offline data to accelerate online visual RL fine-tuning.

Extensive and thorough empirical evaluation across 72 visuomotor continuous control tasks (50 from Meta-World and 22 from DeepMind Control Suite), demonstrating consistent and significant gains in sample efficiency over both train-from-scratch methods (DreamerV3, DrQ-v2) and offline-data baselines (R3M, ExPLORe, UDS-RLPD, JSRL-BC, iVideoGPT).

Clear diagnosis of the failure mode of naive world model fine-tuning (catastrophic forgetting and support mismatch between offline data and online rollouts) accompanied by intuitive and effective mitigating mechanisms (experience rehearsal and execution guidance).
Detailed ablations investigating individual component contributions, retrieval precision, sensitivity to schedule hyperparameters, and robustness against task-irrelevant data injection.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is relatively incremental: the framework integrates known paradigms, namely RSSM-based world models, visual embedding retrieval, and behavior-cloned policy jump-starting / execution mixing (closely following JSRL).

The theoretical contributions in Appendix B are trivial: Proposition 1 is tautological by definition (selecting samples within an epsilon-ball around the online distribution naturally yields a smaller expected distance than the uncurated mixture), and Proposition 2 is a direct restatement of Theorem 4.1 from Kakade & Langford (2002).

The trajectory retrieval mechanism relies solely on initial observation embeddings (Equation 5). This heuristic may break down in settings where diverse downstream tasks share identical initial scenes (e.g., multi-task table setups where goals are defined non-visually or via instructions), although the ablation in Figure 14 partially demonstrates robustness to irrelevant data.

While the dataset is multi-embodiment and mixed-quality, it remains synthetic in-domain data generated by noisy agents in MuJoCo. Validating the framework on truly heterogeneous or real-world robotic demonstration data would further strengthen the claims.

strengths: Compelling and realistic problem setting: Addressing how to effectively leverage reward-free, mixed-quality, multi-embodiment offline data to accelerate online visual RL is highly practical and tackles key bottlenecks in foundation world model deployment.

Extensive and thorough empirical evaluation: The paper conducts benchmark experiments across 72 pixel-based continuous control tasks spanning DMControl and Meta-World. This is substantially broader than typical offline-to-online or world-model control papers.

Strong empirical gains: NCRL achieves roughly double the aggregate score of standard learning-from-scratch baselines (DreamerV3, DrQ-v2) at 150k steps, matching their performance at 500k–1M steps, and clearly outperforms recent offline/pre-training baselines (R3M, UDS-RLPD, ExPLORe, JSRL-BC, iVideoGPT).

Comprehensive ablations and diagnostics: The paper provides informative ablations dissecting the contributions of world model pre-training, experience rehearsal, and execution guidance, along with sensitivity analyses to scheduling, retrieval noise degradation, and model parameter scaling.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is somewhat composite/incremental: The core algorithmic components—unsupervised RSSM pre-training, latent feature nearest-neighbor retrieval via Faiss, and BC-guided rollout execution—are largely adaptations and combinations of existing techniques (Dreamer, standard retrieval, and JSRL variants) rather than fundamentally new algorithmic formulations.

Heuristic nature of the retrieval mechanism: Retrieval relies strictly on Euclidean distance between latent representations of initial observations ($e_\theta(o_{on}^0)$ and $e_\theta(o_{off}^0)$). While this is effective in Meta-World and DMControl where initial states or visual cues distinguish tasks/embodiments, it may fail in settings where initial states are visually identical across different tasks or where diverse camera angles/backgrounds exist.

Evaluation restricted to simulated environments: The empirical validation is conducted entirely within MuJoCo-based simulators (Meta-World, DMControl) with synthetically noisy/exploratory data. Validating the framework on real-world robot demonstrations or large-scale in-the-wild datasets (e.g., Open X-Embodiment, DROID) would significantly strengthen the claims regarding handling truly uncurated data.

Theoretical results offer modest novelty: The theoretical analysis in Appendix B primarily serves as intuitive justification; Proposition 1 is an immediate consequence of epsilon-thresholded subset partitioning, and Proposition 2 is a direct restatement/application of Theorem 4.1 from Kakade & Langford (2002).
